title: Observability Bridge and Execution Surface Manual
author: Priya Nambiar
content:
Purpose

This document defines the Observability Bridge: the cross-cutting contract between the serving runtime execution surface, kernel scheduler, and the observability/benchmarks systems. It is a practical manual for engineers who implement instrumentation, create profiling experiments, debug production SLO regressions, and author synthetic benchmarks.

Scope and audience

- Scope: runtime telemetry schema, kernel scheduling knobs that affect signals, profiling/playbook templates, benchmarking harness integration, incident runbook steps for SLO regressions, and a short release-notes checklist for telemetry changes.
- Audience: runtime engineers, platform SREs, profiling owners, and applied ML engineers onboarding to inferencing performance work.

High-level goals

1. Provide a stable, low-cost telemetry surface that supports causal latency attribution and cost-per-token accounting.
2. Ensure kernel scheduler decisions are visible and actionable in traces, metrics, and sample profiles.
3. Reduce investigation time for tail latency and regression hunts by 50% through standardized probes and playbooks.

Key concepts and terminology

- Execution surface: API boundary between the front-end request router and the per-GPU kernel worker. Includes request metadata (route, priority, model-variant), session affinity hints, and requested QoS profile.
- Kernel epoch: a contiguous sequence of kernel launches that service a single logical request (can include kernel hedges, fallback kernels, and prefetch kernels).
- Decision trace: a compact, append-only event bundle attached to each request that records scheduling choices, cache hits/misses, kernel variant selection, and routing fallbacks.
- Observability Bridge: the canonical set of telemetry artifacts (metrics, traces, event logs, binary samples) and the mapping rules from runtime artifacts to downstream stores (Prometheus, Jaeger/OTel, ClickHouse).

Observability Bridge: telemetry contracts

1) Minimal per-request trace model (OTel-compatible)

- Required attributes (always present):
  - request.id (string)
  - request.route (string)
  - user.tier (string)
  - model.name (string)
  - model.variant (string)
  - sequence.length (int)
  - priority (int)
  - kernel.epoch_id (string)
  - kernel.epoch_stage (enum: enqueue|dispatch|kernel_start|kernel_end|postprocess)

- Important events (emit as spans or events inside the request trace):
  - kvcache.hit / kvcache.miss (include shard_id and approximate latency_ms)
  - kernel.selection (selected_variant, heuristics_triggered)
  - kernel.hedge (hedge_target_ms)
  - routing.fallback (reason_code, fallback_variant)
  - admission.control (slot_granted, preemption_note)

2) Lightweight counters and histograms (Prometheus)

- Counters: requests_total{route,model,variant,priority}, kvcache_hits_total{shard}, kernel_launches_total{variant}, preemptions_total{reason}.
- Histograms/Summaries: request_latency_ms_bucket{route,percentile}, kernel_exec_ms_bucket{variant,slot_type}, kv_latency_ms_bucket{shard}.

3) Binary sample capture (for root-cause)

- Samples must be probabilistic and cost-aware. Default policy: sample 0.1% of requests globally, 1% of requests in the 95–99.9th latency percentile, and 100% of requests marked as incidents. Captured artifacts: full trace, kernel microprofile (CUDA CUPTI / ROCm HSA), and model logits snapshot (first 64 tokens).

Mapping and retention

- Mapping rules: traces -> Jaeger/OTel; counters/histograms -> Prometheus/Thanos; binary samples -> ClickHouse S3-backed archive with TTL 90 days for non-incident samples, 540 days for incident samples.

Kernel scheduler observability patterns

Make scheduling decisions visible without exposing implementation internals:

- Annotate every kernel launch with kernel.metadata tags: slot_type (dedicated|burst|preemptible), kernel_priority, preemptible_till.
- Emit scheduling decisions as events in the request trace with reason codes mapped to stable enum values.
- Surface per-slot occupancy metrics with 1s resolution and 1m rollups.

Example kernel decision trace (OTel pseudo-JSON)

{
  "trace_id": "...",
  "spans": [
    {"name": "request.dispatch", "attributes": {"kernel.epoch_id": "e-6bd3"}},
    {"name": "scheduler.decide", "attributes": {"slot_type": "preemptible", "decision": "queued", "reason": "burst_quota"}},
    {"name": "kernel.launch", "attributes": {"variant": "int8-fastpath", "exec_ms": 12}}
  ]
}

Profiling playbook (quick start)

Purpose: binary reproducible steps to attribute tail latency to one of the common buckets (queuing, kvcache, kernel, postprocess/IO).

1. Reproduce load shape in the local benchmark harness. Use the Operational Workload Simulator (see benchmarking catalog).
2. Run fast-path sampling: collect request traces at 1% sampling for 15 minutes with kernel microprofiles.
3. Run deterministic microbenchmarks: kernel alone, shader-only with identical input sizes, and KV cache-only hit/miss experiments.
4. Apply the causal attribution checklist: correlate request-level latency with kernel.exec_ms, kvcache latency, and scheduler.queue_ms.

Benchmarking harness integration

- Standard artifact: workload YAML describing request distribution, concurrency, model variant mix, and token-length histogram. Example:

workload: "chat-service-small-burst"
concurrency: 120
model_mix: {"gpt-like-xxs": 0.7, "gpt-like-slim": 0.3}
percentile_targets: [50, 95, 99, 99.9]
sequence_length_histogram: "path/to/histogram.json"

- Run sequence:
  1) dry-run (validate connections and KV cache priming)
  2) steady-state ramp to target concurrency over 180s
  3) 10m stable measurement window with live counters and trace sampling
  4) cool-down and artifact collection

- Cost accounting: ensure the harness reports per-token GPU-time and model-variant per-token energy. Use the runtime cost plugin to collect per-token CUDA ns.

Release notes and telemetry changes checklist

- If a PR changes any emitted attribute, add an entry to the telemetry changelog and bump the schema minor version. Mandatory reviewer: Observability Platform (Maya Patel).
- Backwards compatibility rule: new attributes may be added; renaming or removing attributes requires a deprecation cycle of at least 30 days and a coordinated rollout across consumers.

Known issues and mitigations (engineers should copy these patterns into incidents)

1. Symptom: Intermittent 99.9th latency spikes with high kvcache misses.
   - Probable cause: Shard imbalanced eviction or prefetch turned off during burst.
   - Mitigation: Temporarily increase kvcache.repair_concurrency to 8 and enable shard-prefetch for affected route.

2. Symptom: Kernel launch queue grows but kernel.exec_ms stays constant.
   - Probable cause: Admission control or slot exhaustion.
   - Mitigation: Check slot occupancy metrics, temporarily enable burst capacity pool, and scale Dedicated pool if sustained.

3. Symptom: Traces show many scheduler.decide events with reason=preemption_expected.
   - Probable cause: aggressive priority shaping or degraded NVLink.
   - Mitigation: Lower preemption aggressiveness, kick off NVLink health-check job, and route critical traffic to reserved slots.

Incident runbook (SLO regression — high-level)

1) Triage
  - Confirm SLO breach (duration, route, model). Pull top-100 traces for the breach window.
2) Classify
  - Run the profiling playbook reproduction for the same load shape. Compute attribution across queuing, kernel, kv, postprocess.
3) Short-term mitigations
  - Route critical customers to alternate variant/model (prefer lower-latency variant). Throttle bulk routes. Increase sample rate.
4) Root-cause and fix
  - If kernel-related: apply kernel rollback or tuning and run canary. If kvcache-related: rebalance shards and pre-warm hot keys.
5) Postmortem and follow-up
  - Publish incident notes, update telemetry mapping if additional attributes were required, and add a permanent alert if the event repeats.

Operational dashboards and alerts (recommended)

- Dashboards:
  - Runtime Overview: requests/s, 95/99/99.9 latencies, kernel_launch_rate, kvcache_hit_rate, slot_occupancy
  - Scheduler Health: per-slot occupancy heatmap, preemption_rate, queue_length trend
  - Sampling Explorer: sampled-traces-per-minute, tail-sample-conversion-rate (sample -> binary sample)

- Alerts (suggested):
  - P1: 99.9 latency breach for >10m AND tail-sample-conversion-rate < 0.1% -> page oncall
  - P2: slot_occupancy > 95% for 3m -> message runtime-scaling channel
  - P3: kvcache_hit_rate drop > 20% in 5m -> create auto-ticket for kvcache-repair job

How to onboard a consumer (team) to the bridge

1. Request access to the telemetry schema and sample traces (file a ticket to observability-platform).
2. Verify client can parse required attributes and run the compliance test harness (small binary producing sample traces).
3. Run a joint benchmark with a runtime engineer to validate the mapping.

Appendix A — telemetry attribute enum table

| Attribute | Type | Description | Stable values / notes |
| request.route | string | Logical route name | freeform but align to routing service naming |
| kernel.epoch_stage | enum | Stage within epoch | enqueue, dispatch, kernel_start, kernel_end, postprocess |
| slot_type | string | Slot allocation type | dedicated, burst, preemptible |
| preemption_reason | string | High-level reason code | quota_burst, topology_eviction, maintenance |

Appendix B — example CLI snippets

# Run a local sampling session (harness)
redwood-bench run --workload path/to/workload.yaml --sample-rate 0.01 --collect-traces

# Export top traces to local dir
redwood-observe export --time-window "2026-02-08T14:00:00Z/2026-02-08T14:10:00Z" --filter "route=chat-service" --dest ./samples
